newsitem.title: USA: Clinton rides high, Dole says "I'm baffled".
newsitem.headline: Clinton rides high, Dole says "I'm baffled".

text.p: President Bill Clinton took credit for a declining federal deficit on Monday as Republican Bob Dole lamented the apparent disinterest of voters in alleged Clinton White House scandals.

"I'm baffled, I really am baffled ... If the American people really care and they're really concerned about who's in charge, something ought to get their attention sooner or later," Dole said in an interview with CNN.

Dole, frustrated by the indifference to his sharp attacks on the president's conduct with just eight days to go until the November 5 election, speculated that perhaps the voters were confused by the sheer number of Clinton controversies.
The Reuters daily tracking poll showed the president holding a steady lead of more than 13 percentage points over Dole -- enough for a huge victory if the numbers hold.
In University City, Missouri, Clinton took credit for new figures showing a further decline in the U.S. budget deficit, saying it was evidence his economic policies were working.
On the steps of city hall, he stood in front of a large chart showing the country's red ink spending was $290 billion in 1992 when he was elected and had declined every year since.

Two teenagers joined him to pull a string unveiling the deficit figure for the 1996 budget year that ends on Oct. 31. It was $107 billion, the lowest figure since 1981, Republican Ronald Reagan's first year as president.
"We all know that our budget would be in surplus today if it weren't for the interest we pay on the debt rung up in the 12 years before I took office," Clinton said.
Republicans, who have controlled Congress for the last two years, tried to take credit for the deficit decline, claiming their drive to cut federal spending forced the figure down.
Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich of Ohio said that "this accomplishment comes as good news to every American but a complete surprise to Bill Clinton who should get absolutely no credit for it."
Republican Party Chairman Haley Barbour told reporters: "This is a huge credit to the common sense Republican Congress which fought for spending constraints."

Reflecting fears Dole may be headed for a big defeat, the Republican Party opened a multi-million dollar TV ad blitz aimed at keeping their hold on the House of Representatives, which they won in 1994 after 40 years in the minority.

The advertisement warned voters against re-electing Clinton with a Democratic Congress, saying the Democrats in 1993 and 1994 produced "the largest tax increase in history ... more wasteful Washington spending ... a government run health care scheme."
Dole himself has become more shrill on the campaign trail in the past week. In a rally in California on Saturday, he said he could not believe American voters would re-elect Clinton
"They've turned the White House into something else -- the animal house," he charged.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Dole was flailing because he was losing. "It's increasingly becoming less necessary to respond as the shrillness and the absurdity of the remarks accelerates," McCurry said.

There was little sign that a last-gasp Dole effort to win in California was producing results. A Los Angeles Times poll in predominantly Republican Orange County showed him virtually tied with Clinton. Republicans normally need to carry the county by 250,000 votes or more to win the state.

Meanwhile Republicans continued to turn their backs on their nominee. Media adviser Don Sipple, who left the Dole campaign last month, told Newsweek Dole was stuck in the 1950s and 1960s and would not make a good president.
